articles.title: TOEFL iBT format at a glance
lines: Since 21 January 2026 the TOEFL iBT has a new, shorter format. It still has four sections (Reading, Listening, Writing and Speaking), but the tasks are shorter, two sections adapt to your level, and scores are reported on a 1-6 band scale. This page is the one-screen summary. The other articles in this group go deeper into each point.
## The four sections
- Reading: 50 items, about 30 minutes. Two-stage adaptive.
- Listening: 47 items, about 29 minutes. Two-stage adaptive.
- Writing: 12 items, 23 minutes. Ten Build a Sentence items, one Write an Email, one Write for an Academic Discussion.
- Speaking: 11 items, 8 minutes. Seven Listen and Repeat items and four Take an Interview questions with 45 seconds per answer.

The actual testing time is roughly 1 hour 23 minutes to 1 hour 29 minutes. With check-in, directions and screens between tasks, plan for about 2 hours in total. There is no scheduled break, so eat, drink and use the bathroom before you start.
## Reading tasks
- Complete the Words: a short academic paragraph in which some words are cut in half. You type the missing letters. It tests spelling, word forms and grammar in context.
- Read in Daily Life: short everyday texts such as an email, a notice, a menu, a text message chain or a web page, each with a few questions.
- Read an Academic Passage: a passage of about 200 words on a university topic, followed by several questions on main idea, detail, inference, vocabulary and purpose.
## Listening tasks
- Listen and Choose a Response: you hear one line and choose the most natural reply from four written options.
- Conversations: short campus or daily-life exchanges between two people.
- Announcements: a speaker gives information to a group, such as a change to a schedule.
- Academic Talks: a short lecture-style talk on a university subject.
Every recording is played once. The questions appear after the recording, so you must listen well and take short notes.
## Writing tasks

- Build a Sentence: you see a short exchange and must put word chunks in the right order to make the reply. It tests word order: questions, indirect questions, auxiliaries, relative clauses, passives and adverbs.
- Write an Email: you read a situation and three points to cover, then write a polite email to a professor, a manager, a landlord or a service.
- Write for an Academic Discussion: a professor posts a question to an online class, two students reply, and you add your own contribution with a clear opinion and reasons.
## Speaking tasks
- Listen and Repeat: you hear a sentence and repeat it as exactly as you can. Sentences get longer as you go.
- Take an Interview: an interviewer asks four questions on one topic, moving from your experience to your opinion. You have 45 seconds for each answer.
## Adaptive Reading and Listening

Reading and Listening each start with a router module that everyone takes. Your performance there decides whether your second module is a lower or an upper module. The upper module has harder material and lets you reach the top bands. Some items in the test are unscored (they are being tried out for future tests), and you cannot tell which ones, so treat every item as if it counts.
## Scores in one paragraph

Each section gets a band from 1 to 6 in half steps (1, 1.5, 2 ... 6), aligned to the CEFR levels used by many universities. Your overall score is the average of the four section bands, rounded to the nearest half band. For two years after January 2026, ETS also shows a comparable score on the old 0-120 scale so institutions can compare. There is no pass or fail: each university or employer sets its own requirement.
## Where you can take it

You can take the test at a test center or at home with TOEFL iBT Home Edition, which uses a live remote proctor. Note-taking is allowed. Fees, ID rules and the equipment needed for Home Edition change from time to time, so always check them on ets.org before you register.
! The most common surprise on test day is the pace. The tasks are short and they come quickly, one after another, with no break. Practice full mocks in one sitting so the rhythm feels normal.
## How this app matches the test

The mock tests in this app follow the same sections, task types, item counts and timings, and the Reading and Listening mocks route you to a lower or upper module based on your first module. Use the section practice to learn each task type, then take full mocks to build speed and stamina.

articles.title: What changed in January 2026
lines: If you studied for the TOEFL before 2026, or you are using an older prep book or older videos, a lot of what you learned is out of date. The test that began on 21 January 2026 has different tasks, different timing and a different score scale. This article lists what changed and what it means for how you prepare.
## Shorter tasks, more of them

The older test used fewer, longer tasks: long reading passages with many questions each, long lectures, and integrated speaking and writing tasks that combined reading, listening and a spoken or written response. The new test breaks the skills into many short items. Reading now has 50 items in about 30 minutes, and Listening has 47 items in about 29 minutes. You move faster and see a wider range of texts and speakers.
- Long passages have been replaced by short academic passages of about 200 words, plus everyday texts and the Complete the Words task.
- Long lectures have been replaced by short academic talks, announcements, conversations and single-line Listen and Choose a Response items.
- Speaking is now 8 minutes: Listen and Repeat plus a four-question interview.
- Writing is now 23 minutes: Build a Sentence, Write an Email and Write for an Academic Discussion.
## Adaptive Reading and Listening

Reading and Listening are now two-stage adaptive. Everyone takes a router module first; depending on how you do, you then get a lower or an upper second module. In the old test, everyone saw the same level of difficulty. Now the first module really matters, because it opens the door to the harder module where the highest bands are possible.
! Do not slow down in the router module to be perfect on every item. Accuracy matters, but so does finishing. Work carefully and steadily, and never leave an item blank.
## New task types
- Complete the Words is new. It rewards strong spelling, grammar and knowledge of word families (analyze, analysis, analytical).
- Read in Daily Life is new. It uses practical texts such as notices, emails and schedules, not only academic material.
- Listen and Choose a Response is new. It tests whether you understand natural spoken English, including indirect replies.
- Build a Sentence is new. It tests word order directly.
- Write an Email is new. It tests practical, polite written communication.
- Listen and Repeat and Take an Interview replace the old speaking tasks. There is no longer a task where you read, listen and then summarize.
The Academic Discussion writing task existed in the 2023-2025 version and remains, so any practice you did on it is still useful.
## A new score scale

Old scores were 0-30 per section and 0-120 in total. New scores are bands from 1 to 6 in half steps for each section, and the overall score is the average of the four, rounded to the nearest half band. The bands are aligned to the CEFR (A1 to C2). For two years after January 2026, score reports also give a comparable 0-120 score, so universities that still publish requirements on the old scale can compare. See "Scores, bands and CEFR" for the full conversion table.
## What did not change
- It is still an English test for university study, with academic content in all sections.
- You can still take it at a test center or at home with Home Edition and a live remote proctor.
- Notes are still allowed.
- Scores are still valid for 2 years, and you can still send free score reports and use MyBest scores.
- There is still no pass or fail. Each institution decides what score it needs.
## What this means for your preparation
- Throw away timing plans built for the old test. Long-passage strategies such as reading the whole passage first and then answering 10 questions do not fit 200-word passages.
- Practice speed. Many short items mean less time to think about each one.
- Train your ear for natural, everyday English, not just lectures. Announcements, conversations and quick replies are a big part of Listening.
- Practice spelling and word forms for Complete the Words, and word order for Build a Sentence.
- For Speaking, train short-term memory and pronunciation (Listen and Repeat) and fluent 45-second answers (Interview).
- Check your target universities' requirements again. Many now give a band score, some still give an old 0-120 score, and some give both.

! If a prep book or video mentions integrated speaking, integrated writing, or section scores out of 30, it describes the old test. Its grammar and vocabulary advice may still help, but ignore its task strategies and timing.

articles.title: Scores, bands and CEFR: how to read your mock score
lines: The new TOEFL iBT reports every section on a band scale from 1 to 6, in half bands. This article explains how the bands work, how the overall score is calculated, how bands relate to the old 0-120 scale and to the CEFR, and how to read the score this app gives you after a mock test.
## Section bands and the overall score

Each section (Reading, Listening, Writing, Speaking) gets a band: 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6. Your overall score is the average of the four section bands, rounded to the nearest half band.
> Reading 5, Listening 4.5, Writing 4.5, Speaking 4. Total 18, divided by 4 = 4.5. Overall: 4.5.
> Reading 5, Listening 5, Writing 5, Speaking 4.5. Total 19.5, divided by 4 = 4.875. Rounded to the nearest half band: 5.

Notice that one weak section pulls the overall score down, and one strong section can lift it. Many universities also set a minimum for each section, so check both numbers in your target's requirements.
## Bands and the CEFR
The bands are aligned to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), the scale many universities and visa systems use. Roughly:
- 6 = C2 (mastery)
- 5 and 5.5 = C1 (advanced)
- 4 and 4.5 = B2 (upper intermediate)
- 3 and 3.5 = B1 (intermediate)
- 2 and 2.5 = A2 (elementary)
- 1 and 1.5 = A1 (beginner)
Many undergraduate and graduate programs ask for something in the B2 to C1 range, but requirements vary widely, so always check the exact figure your target institution publishes.
## Converting from the old 0-120 scale
For two years after January 2026, ETS also reports a comparable 0-120 total. If a university still lists a requirement on the old scale, use this concordance (old total to new overall band):
- 114 and above = 6
> A program asks for 90 on the old scale. 90 falls in the 86-94 range, which matches band 4.5. Aim for 4.5 overall at least, and preferably a little higher to be safe.

! Do not convert in your head and stop there. If the university states its requirement in bands, use the bands. If it states it on the old scale, check the comparable 0-120 score on your official report. If in doubt, ask the admissions office which number they will look at.
## When and how you get your scores
- Scores appear in your ETS account about 3 days after the test.
- Scores are valid for 2 years.
- You can send 4 free score reports. You must choose the institutions by 10 pm on test day. Extra reports cost US$25 each.
- MyBest scores show your best result for each section from your valid tests, and some institutions accept them. Ask each institution whether it does.
- There is no pass or fail. A score is only "enough" or "not enough" for a particular program.
## How to read your mock score in this app

After each full mock, the app shows a band for each section and an overall band calculated the same way as the real test (average of four, rounded to the nearest half band). Keep these points in mind:
- Mock scores are estimates. They come from practice material, not from ETS, so treat them as a guide to your level, not a promise.
- Reading and Listening bands depend on which second module you reached. If the app routed you to the lower module, your possible band is capped; reaching the upper module is the first goal.

- Writing and Speaking bands in a practice app are harder to estimate than Reading and Listening. Compare your answers with the model answers and the checklists, and if possible ask a teacher or a strong English speaker to review a few.
- One mock is one data point. Look at the trend over three or more mocks before changing your plan.
## Turning a score into a target
- Write down your target overall band and any section minimums.
- Compare them with your latest mock. Which section is furthest below its target?
- Put most of your study time into that section, but do not let your strongest section slip.
- Re-test with a full mock every one or two weeks. See "Using your mock results" for a step-by-step review method.

! A gap of half a band can often be closed in a few weeks with focused work. A gap of one and a half bands or more usually needs a longer plan and more daily practice. Be realistic when you book your test date.

articles.title: Registering, test day and Home Edition checklist
lines: Good preparation can be wasted by a problem on test day: the wrong ID, a computer that fails the check, or arriving late. This checklist covers what to do before you register, the week before, and on the day, for both test centers and Home Edition. Rules change, so treat this as a reminder list and confirm every detail on ets.org.
## Before you register
- Check what each target institution needs: the overall band, any section minimums, whether it accepts Home Edition, whether it accepts MyBest scores, and its application deadline.
- Work backward from the earliest deadline. Scores reach your ETS account about 3 days after the test, and institutions may take longer to process them. Leave time for a second attempt if possible.
- Decide between a test center and Home Edition. A test center gives you a controlled room and equipment. Home Edition saves travel but needs a suitable room, computer and internet connection.
- Check the current fee, payment options and rescheduling rules on ets.org. They differ by country and change over time.
- Check the ID rules for your country on ets.org. The name on your registration must match your ID exactly, so check spelling, the order of names and any middle name.
! Make sure the name in your ETS account matches your passport or other accepted ID letter for letter. A mismatch is one of the most common reasons test takers are turned away.
## Score reports

You can send 4 free score reports, and you must choose the institutions by 10 pm on test day. Prepare the list of institutions (and their codes, if required) before the test so you do not have to decide in a hurry. Extra reports cost US$25 each.
## The week before
- Take your last full mock no later than 2 or 3 days before the test, so you are not tired on the day.
- Review your notes on templates for Write an Email and Academic Discussion, and your Interview answer pattern.
- Plan the route to the test center and the travel time, or set up and test your Home Edition room.
- Sleep at your normal time. Do not try to learn large lists of new words in the last two days.
## Home Edition checklist

Home Edition is the same test taken on your own computer with a live remote proctor watching through your webcam. Check the exact equipment and room requirements on ets.org, and run any system check ETS provides well before test day and again the day before. In general you should expect to need:
- A computer that meets ETS requirements (check which operating systems and browsers are supported).
- A working webcam, microphone and speaker or headphones as allowed by the rules.
- A stable internet connection. If possible, use a wired connection and ask others at home not to stream video during your test.
- A quiet, private room with a clear desk and a closed door. Nobody else may enter during the test.
- An accepted ID document.
- Approved note-taking materials. Check on ets.org what is allowed at home, because it may be different from a test center.

! Power cuts and slow internet are real risks in many places. Charge your laptop fully, keep it plugged in, and if load shedding is common in your area, check the schedule and book a time when power is most reliable or consider a test center.
## Test center checklist
- Confirm the address, arrival time and what you may bring.
- Bring your accepted ID. Keep it with you until check-in.
- Arrive early. Late arrival can mean you are not allowed to test.
- Expect your personal items, including your phone, to be stored away during the test.
- Note-taking materials are normally provided at the center; do not bring your own paper unless the rules say you may.
## On the day
- Eat a normal meal and drink some water. There is no scheduled break, and the whole session takes about 2 hours including check-in and directions.
- Use the bathroom before you start.
- Wear comfortable clothes in layers; rooms can be cold or warm.
- During the test, follow the on-screen timer, not your own estimate.
- If something goes wrong (a sound problem, a frozen screen), tell the proctor or administrator at once rather than trying to fix it yourself.
## After the test
- Choose your free score report recipients by 10 pm on test day if you have not already.
- Check your ETS account for scores about 3 days later.
- If your score is below target, review it by section and plan your next attempt with the "Using your mock results" method.

articles.title: Adaptive modules explained
lines: Reading and Listening on the new TOEFL iBT are two-stage adaptive. That sounds technical, but the idea is simple, and understanding it changes how you should approach the first part of each section.
## How the two stages work
- Stage 1 is the router module. Every test taker gets a module of mixed difficulty.
- Your performance in the router decides your stage 2 module.
- If you do well, you get the upper module, with harder texts, faster or more complex speech and more inference questions.
- If you do less well, you get the lower module, with more accessible material.

Your band for the section is based on both modules. The upper module is the route to the top bands; the lower module limits how high your band can go. This is why the router is so important: it is your chance to show the test you belong in the upper module.
## What adaptive does not mean
- It does not change item by item. The level is chosen once, between the two modules, not after every question.
- It does not punish you for seeing hard questions. In the upper module, hard items are expected and you are not supposed to get them all right.
- It does not mean an easy second module is "good news". If stage 2 feels much easier than stage 1, you were probably routed to the lower module.
! Do not try to guess which module you are in while you are testing. It wastes attention. Just answer each item as well as you can.
## Unscored items

Some items in the test are unscored: ETS is trying them out for future tests. They look exactly like normal items and you cannot tell which ones they are. Never skip an item because you think it might not count.
## Strategy for the router module
- Start focused. Many test takers lose points in the first few minutes because they are nervous or still settling in. Take one slow breath before you begin and read the first directions carefully.
- Do not rush the easy items. Careless mistakes on simple questions hurt more in the router, because they can send you to the lower module.
- Do not spend too long on one hard item either. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, choose the best remaining option and move on.
- Answer every item. A blank answer is always wrong; a guess may be right.
- In Complete the Words, check spelling and word endings (plural -s, past -ed, -tion versus -sion). Small slips add up.
## Strategy for stage 2
- If the module feels hard, that is a good sign. Stay calm and keep using your method.
- Expect longer or denser texts, more paraphrase between the text and the correct option, and wrong options that are partly true.
- If the module feels easy, do not relax too much. Collect every point you can: accuracy here still raises your band within its range.
## How the app simulates this

The full mocks in this app also use a router module and then a lower or upper module, chosen by your router result. After each mock, note which module you reached in Reading and in Listening. Use this as one of your main progress signs:
- If you reach the lower module, focus on accuracy in the most common item types and on careless errors.
- If you reach the upper module but your band is not rising, focus on harder skills: inference, purpose questions, vocabulary in context and tricky distractors.

> Example: Amara reaches the lower Reading module in her first two mocks. Her review shows she misses half of the Complete the Words items because of spelling and word-form errors, and she runs out of time on the last academic passage. She practices word families daily and sets a time check halfway through the module. In her third mock she reaches the upper module.
## Common myths
- "The first questions are worth more." Not in the way people think. What matters is your overall performance in the router, not just the first few items.
- "If I see a hard question, I must have got the last one right." The router has mixed difficulty by design, so you cannot read your performance from the next item.
- "I can't change my score after the router." You can. Your stage 2 performance still moves your band up or down within the range of that module.
! The best adaptive strategy is the boring one: steady, careful work from the very first item to the last, with no blanks.

articles.title: Time management section by section
lines: The new TOEFL is short, but it is fast. Many test takers know enough English to score well and still lose points because they spend too long on a few items and then rush the rest. This article gives you a time plan for each section and simple habits to keep it.
## The big picture
- Reading: 50 items in about 30 minutes, an average of well under a minute per item.
- Listening: 47 items in about 29 minutes, but much of that time is spent listening. You answer after each recording, so the pace is partly set for you.
- Writing: 12 items in 23 minutes, with most of the time going to the two writing tasks.
- Speaking: 11 items in 8 minutes. The timing is fully controlled by the test; your job is to use it well.
! Always follow the on-screen timer. Your sense of time changes under stress.
## Reading

Different item types take different amounts of time. Complete the Words items are quick once you have read the paragraph; Read in Daily Life questions are moderate; academic passage questions take the longest.
- Complete the Words: read the whole paragraph quickly first for meaning, then fill the gaps. Do not stop for long on a single word; come back to it if the module lets you.
- Read in Daily Life: read the questions first, then scan the text for each answer. These texts are short and practical.
- Academic Passage: skim the passage for the main idea (about 30-45 seconds), then answer the questions, going back to the relevant sentence for each one.
- Set a checkpoint: at about half the module time, you should be roughly halfway through the items. If you are behind, speed up on the next easy items.
- Never leave a blank. If time is almost over, choose an answer for every remaining item.
## Listening
- You hear each recording once. Before it starts, read anything on screen that tells you the context (who is talking, what kind of talk it is).
- Answer each question promptly. Long hesitation does not improve your memory of the recording.
- If you do not know an answer, eliminate options that contradict your notes or were not mentioned, choose, and move on. The next recording needs your full attention.
## Writing
A practical split for 23 minutes:

- Build a Sentence (10 items): work quickly and keep moving. Find the start of the sentence (often the subject or the question word), then the verb, then the rest. Check the full sentence reads naturally before you go on.
- Write an Email (7 minutes): about 1 minute to read and plan, 5 minutes to write, 1 minute to check.
- Academic Discussion (10 minutes): about 1-2 minutes to read and choose a position, 7 minutes to write, 1 minute to check.
! Save one minute at the end of each writing task to check. Fixing a wrong verb form or a missing article is quick and visible to the scorer.
## Speaking
- Listen and Repeat: focus completely during the sentence. Start speaking as soon as you are allowed, while the sentence is still fresh. Keep your pace natural.
- Interview: 45 seconds is short. Give your answer in the first sentence, then one reason and one example. If you finish early, add a second example or a short conclusion. Do not stop at 20 seconds.
> Interview timing: 0-5 s answer ("I'd say I prefer studying in the morning."), 5-25 s reason and example, 25-40 s extra detail or comparison, 40-45 s short closing sentence.
## Training your sense of time
- Practice with the timer on from the first week, even in section practice.
- Write your finishing time on each practice set. Watch the number go down.
- In full mocks, note where you lost time. Was it one academic passage? The Build a Sentence items? Fix that one place next week.
- Learn to let go. If one item has taken twice the average time, guess and move on. One item is never worth three.
## A note on stamina

There is no scheduled break, so your concentration must last the whole session. Late in the test, people read more slowly and make more careless errors. Full mocks in one sitting train this. See "Test anxiety and stamina".

articles.title: Note-taking for Listening
lines: In Listening, every recording is played once and the questions appear after it. Notes help you remember the main idea, the structure and key details. But notes can also hurt: if you write too much, you stop listening. This article shows how to take short, useful notes for each type of recording.
## The rules of good test notes
- Write less than you think. Key words, not sentences.
- Listen first, write second. If you are writing while the speaker says something important, you will miss it.
- Use the left side of the page for main points and indent details under them.
- Use symbols and short forms you already know well. Test day is not the time to invent a new system.
- Leave space. A crowded page is hard to read in the few seconds you have.
## Useful symbols and short forms
- up arrow or + : increase, more, positive
- down arrow or - : decrease, less, negative
- -> : causes, leads to, results in
- = : means, is the same as
- vs : contrast, compared with
- b/c : because
- e.g. : example
- ex : exception or example (choose one and keep it)
- ? : speaker is unsure, or a question is raised
- ! : speaker stresses this point
- M / W : man / woman in a conversation
- P / S : professor / student
> Notes for a sentence like "The professor explains that bees communicate where food is located by a special movement, and the angle of this movement tells other bees the direction" might be:
> bees comm. food loc. -> dance
>   angle = direction
## What to listen for in each recording type
## Conversations

Note who has the problem and what it is, the solution or options discussed, and what the person decides to do. Questions often ask about the main purpose of the conversation, a detail, the speaker's attitude, or what they will do next.
> W: can't register - class full
> M: ask prof -> waitlist? / other section Thurs
> W: will email prof today
## Announcements
Note what is changing, when, where, and what listeners must do. Announcements often contain one key instruction.
> library 3rd floor closed - repairs - next week
> study rooms -> 2nd floor
> book online first
## Academic talks
Note the topic, the main point, the examples, and any contrast. Questions often ask about the main idea and why the speaker mentions an example.
> topic: coral bleaching
> cause: water temp up -> algae leave
> ex: reef recovers if temp drops quickly
> contrast: long heat -> coral dies
## Listen and Choose a Response
These are single lines, so you usually do not need notes at all. Focus on the speaker's purpose: is it a question, an offer, a complaint, a piece of news? The best reply often answers indirectly.
> "Do you want to get coffee after the seminar?" A natural reply: "I wish I could, but I have to finish my lab report."
## Listening signals that tell you what to write
- Topic signals: "Today we're going to look at...", "So, the question is..."
- Example signals: "For instance...", "Take ... as an example."
- Contrast signals: "However...", "But here's the thing...", "On the other hand..."
- Importance signals: "The key point is...", "What really matters here...", "Remember this..."
- Change of mind: "Actually...", "Wait, I just remembered..." In conversations, the final decision matters more than the first idea.
! When you hear "but" or "actually", write down what comes next. The answer to a question is very often after a contrast.
## Practice routine
- Week 1: listen to one recording with no notes and answer the questions. Then listen to another recording and take notes. Compare your scores.
- Week 2: limit yourself to about 10-15 words per academic talk. Check whether your notes still let you answer the main idea and example questions.
- Every day: practice your symbols on English podcasts or university lectures you find online. Five minutes is enough.
- After each practice set, look at the questions you missed. Was the answer in your notes? If not, was it after a signal word you did not notice?
## Home Edition and test center notes
Note-taking is allowed in both formats, but the materials can differ. Check on ets.org what you may use for notes at home before test day, and practice with the same kind of surface.

articles.title: Building academic vocabulary
lines: Vocabulary affects every section. In Reading you need it for Complete the Words and vocabulary-in-context questions; in Listening it helps you follow academic talks; in Writing and Speaking it lets you express ideas precisely. The good news is that a few hundred high-frequency academic words appear again and again across subjects. Learn those well and the test becomes much easier.
## Which words to learn

- General academic words: words used in every subject, such as analyze, significant, assume, factor, approach, evidence, decline, contribute, consequence, distinct, interpret, sufficient. These are your top priority.

- Topic words: the basic terms of common TOEFL subjects (biology, geology, astronomy, history, psychology, economics, art). You do not need specialist knowledge, but words like species, sediment, orbit, settlement, behavior and demand should not surprise you.
- Campus words: words for university life, such as enrollment, deadline, advisor, prerequisite, transcript, dormitory, extension and tuition. These appear in conversations, announcements and emails.
- Signal words: however, therefore, whereas, nevertheless, in contrast, as a result. They show how ideas connect and help you answer purpose and inference questions.
## Learn word families, not single words
Complete the Words tests whether you can finish a word correctly in context, and that depends on the right form. Learn each word with its family.
> analyze (verb), analysis (noun), analyst (person), analytical (adjective)
> vary (verb), variation (noun), variety (noun), various (adjective), variable (adjective, noun)
> economy (noun), economic (adjective, about the economy), economical (adjective, saving money), economist (person)
! Watch for pairs that look alike but mean different things: economic/economical, historic/historical, sensible/sensitive, affect (verb)/effect (noun).
## Learn words in sentences
A word list with translations is a start, but you remember a word much better when you meet it in a sentence. For each new word, write one sentence of your own about your own life or studies.
> "The survey found a significant increase in the number of students cycling to campus."
## Synonyms for vocabulary-in-context questions

Reading questions ask which word is closest in meaning to a word in the passage. The correct option fits the sentence's meaning, not just the dictionary entry. Learn one to three synonyms for each key word, and always check the sentence.
> "The new policy had a marked effect on attendance." Here marked means noticeable or clear, not "written on".
## Collocations for writing and speaking
Collocations are words that naturally go together. Using them makes your writing and speech sound natural.
- make a decision, make progress, make an effort (not do a decision)
- do research, do homework, do damage
- conduct an experiment, raise a question, draw a conclusion
- play a role in, have an impact on, pay attention to
- strongly agree, highly effective, widely used
## A daily vocabulary routine (15-20 minutes)
- Learn 10 new words with the flashcards in this app: meaning, word family, one synonym.
- Review yesterday's words and the words from three days ago and one week ago. Spaced review is the most efficient way to remember.
- Write two sentences using today's words.
- When you read or listen to anything in English, note one or two academic words you meet and add them to your list.
! Ten words a day with honest review beats fifty words a day that you forget by the weekend.
## Guessing meaning from context
You will always meet some unknown words. Use the context:
- Look for a definition or example nearby ("such as", "that is", "in other words").
- Look for contrast ("unlike", "but") which tells you the word means the opposite of something you know.
- Look at word parts: un-, in-, dis- (not), re- (again), pre- (before), -able (can be), -less (without).
> "Unlike the gregarious meerkat, the leopard is largely solitary." If solitary means alone, gregarious must mean social, living in groups.
## Using vocabulary in Writing and Speaking

Do not try to fill your email or discussion post with rare words. Use words you are sure of, correctly. One precise word ("this would reduce traffic") is better than an impressive wrong one. Aim for variety: if you have written "important" twice, try "essential", "crucial" or "significant" the third time.

articles.title: Common mistakes South Asian test takers make
lines: Many test takers from Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal use English every day, at school, at work and online. That is a big advantage. But South Asian English has its own patterns, and some of them are marked as errors on the TOEFL, which follows standard American usage. These are not "bad English"; they are local habits that cost points in a test. This article lists the most common ones with corrections.
## Word order in questions and indirect questions
This matters for Build a Sentence and for every email you write.
> Wrong: Can you tell me where is the library?
> Right: Can you tell me where the library is?
> Wrong: I want to know what time does the lab open.
> Right: I want to know what time the lab opens.
! After "Can you tell me", "Do you know", "I wonder" and "I'd like to know", use statement order: subject, then verb.
> Wrong: Why you didn't come to class?
> Right: Why didn't you come to class?
> Wrong: Always I study in the morning.
> Right: I always study in the morning.
## Articles (a, an, the)
Urdu, Hindi, Bengali and many other South Asian languages do not use articles in the same way, so they are often dropped or added.
> Wrong: She is best student in class.
> Right: She is the best student in the class.
> Wrong: I am going to university to meet professor.
> Right: I am going to the university to meet my professor.
> Wrong: The students need the confidence to speak.
> Right: Students need confidence to speak. (general statement about all students, uncountable noun)
- Use a or an the first time you mention a singular countable thing: a report, an email.
- Use the when the reader knows which one: the report I sent you, the library on campus.
- Use no article for general plural or uncountable nouns: Books are expensive. Information is useful.
## Prepositions
> Wrong: We discussed about the project. Right: We discussed the project.
> Wrong: She is married with an engineer. Right: She is married to an engineer.
> Wrong: I have been here since two years. Right: I have been here for two years.
> Wrong: He is good in math. Right: He is good at math.
> Wrong: Let's meet on the evening. Right: Let's meet in the evening.
> Wrong: I will reach to the campus at nine. Right: I will reach the campus at nine. (or: I will get to the campus at nine.)
## Tense and aspect
> Wrong: I am studying here since 2023. Right: I have been studying here since 2023.
> Wrong: I am having two brothers. Right: I have two brothers.
> Wrong: I am knowing the answer. Right: I know the answer.
> Wrong: Yesterday I have submitted the assignment. Right: Yesterday I submitted the assignment.

! Use the present perfect (have done, have been doing) for something that started in the past and continues now. Use the simple past with a finished time like yesterday, last week or in 2022. Verbs like know, have (own), want, believe and understand are not usually used in the -ing form.
## Countable and uncountable nouns
> Wrong: informations, advices, equipments, furnitures, luggages, researches (as a general noun)
> Right: information, advice, equipment, furniture, luggage, research
> Wrong: one of my friend. Right: one of my friends.
## Local expressions to avoid in test writing
These are widely understood in South Asia but sound unusual or wrong to an international reader.
- "Please do the needful." Say exactly what you need: "Could you please extend the deadline?"
- "I will revert back to you." Say "I will get back to you" or "I will reply soon".
- "Can we prepone the meeting?" Say "Can we move the meeting earlier?"
- "My cousin brother." Say "my cousin".
- "I will come today itself." Say "I will come today" or "I will come later today".
- "I passed out in 2024." Say "I graduated in 2024".
- "What is your good name?" Say "What is your name?" or "May I ask your name?"
- "Kindly" in every sentence. Once is polite; three times sounds odd. Mix in "Could you please..." and "I would appreciate it if...".
## Agreement and question tags
> Wrong: He don't like it. Right: He doesn't like it.
> Wrong: Each of the students have a laptop. Right: Each of the students has a laptop.
> Wrong: You finished the report, isn't it? Right: You finished the report, didn't you?
## Speaking: pronunciation points
Pronunciation does not need to sound American, but it must be clear. Common points to practice:
- v and w: very, west, vowel, wave. Keep them distinct.
- Word stress: deVELop, phoTOGraphy, eCOnomy, deterMINE. Wrong stress can make a word hard to recognize.
- Initial consonant clusters: say "school" and "study", not "iskool" or "istudy".
- Final sounds: do not drop the -s or -ed at the end of words in Listen and Repeat. "She walked" and "she walks" are different sentences.
## How to fix these habits
- Pick three mistakes from this list that you know you make. Write correct example sentences on a card.
- When you check your writing practice, search for those three mistakes first.
- In Listen and Repeat practice, record yourself and compare with the original, word by word.
- Read English written by international writers (news sites, university blogs) to get used to standard usage.

articles.title: Test anxiety and stamina
lines: Feeling nervous before an important test is normal; it shows you care. A little stress can even sharpen your focus. Problems start when nerves make you rush, freeze or lose concentration. Stamina is the other side of the same problem: the TOEFL session lasts about 2 hours with no scheduled break, and your focus must last until the final interview question.
## Why preparation is the best calm

Most test anxiety comes from uncertainty: not knowing what the screens will look like, how fast the tasks come, or whether you will run out of time. Every full mock you take removes some of that uncertainty. By test day you should have seen every task type many times, so nothing surprises you.
- Know the order of sections and tasks.
- Know your plan for each task (what you do first, second, third).
- Know your timing checkpoints.
- Have your email and discussion templates ready in your head.
## Before the test
- Sleep. Two normal nights of sleep before the test matter more than two extra hours of study.
- Do not cram. The day before, do a light review: your templates, your list of personal mistakes, a few vocabulary cards. Then stop.
- Prepare everything the night before: ID, route or Home Edition room, a bottle of water, a light snack for before the test.
- Eat a normal meal a few hours before. Avoid trying new foods or a lot of extra caffeine.
## A 60-second reset you can use anywhere
- Breathe in slowly through your nose for 4 counts.
- Hold for 2 counts.
- Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6 counts.
- Repeat three times.
- Put both feet flat on the floor and notice the chair supporting you.
Use this before the test starts, between sections, or any time you feel your heart racing. A long out-breath tells your body to slow down.
! Practice the breathing reset at home first. A technique you have tried ten times works much better under stress than one you read about once.
## During the test
- Expect one or two hard items in every section. They are normal, especially in the upper module. They do not mean you are failing.
- If you miss something in a recording, let it go. Guess, and give the next recording your full attention. Worrying about the last item costs you the next one.
- Talk to yourself in a calm, practical voice: "Next item. What is the question asking?"
- Keep your shoulders and jaw relaxed. Tension makes you tired faster.
- In Speaking, if you make a mistake, correct it quickly or just keep going. Smooth recovery sounds more fluent than a long pause.
## Building stamina
The session is short compared with older tests, but it is intense. To build the stamina you need:
- Take full mocks in one sitting with no pause, from Reading through Speaking, just like the real test.
- Take them at the same time of day as your real test if possible.
- Do not check your phone between sections during a mock.
- Notice where your accuracy drops. Many people find their mistakes increase in Writing or Speaking because they are tired. If that is you, take more full mocks, not just more section practice.
- Daily habits help: regular sleep, some physical activity, and reading or listening to English for longer periods (20-30 minutes without stopping).
## For Home Edition takers
Testing at home can feel more comfortable but has its own stress: worrying about the internet, noise or the proctor. Reduce it by:
- Doing your system checks early and again the day before.
- Telling everyone at home when your test is and asking for quiet.
- Clearing your desk and room the evening before.
- Logging in early so you are not rushed.
## If the test does not go well

One test does not define you. Many test takers improve on a second attempt because they know exactly what to expect. Review your section scores, compare them with your mock results, and make a focused plan. MyBest scores may also help if your institution accepts them.
! Confidence comes from evidence. Keep a small log of your mock bands and practice scores. On the day before the test, read it and remind yourself how far you have come.

articles.title: Reading tips and tricks
lines: The Reading section has 50 items in about 30 minutes, in a router module and then a lower or upper module. It mixes three task types: Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life and Read an Academic Passage. Here are practical methods for each one, plus the traps to avoid.
## Complete the Words
You see an academic paragraph with some words cut short. You type the missing letters.
- Read the whole paragraph once quickly for meaning before you fill anything. The meaning of the sentence tells you what the word must be.
- Then look at grammar: is the word a noun, verb, adjective or adverb? Singular or plural? Past or present?
- Use the first letters you are given. They limit the options a lot.
- Check spelling carefully. A word that is almost right is still wrong.
> "Many species of birds mig___ south in the autumn to find food." The sentence needs a present plural verb after "species": migrate.
> "The results were surpri___ because nobody expected them." After "were", an adjective is needed: surprising.

! The most common mistakes in this task are word endings: -s for plurals and third person, -ed for past and passive, and noun versus adjective forms (analysis/analytical, success/successful). Check every ending.
## Read in Daily Life
These are short practical texts: emails, notices, schedules, product information, messages.
- Look at the type of text first. An email has a purpose; a notice has an instruction; a schedule has times and places.
- Read the question, then find the part of the text that answers it. You rarely need to read everything twice.
- Watch for conditions and exceptions: "except on weekends", "only for registered members", "unless you have already paid".
- Questions often ask about the purpose of the text, a detail, or what the reader should do next.

> A notice says the gym is closed Monday for cleaning and that members can use the pool as usual. A question asks what members can do on Monday. The answer is "swim", not "use the gym", even though "gym" appears in every option.
## Read an Academic Passage
Passages are about 200 words on a university topic, with several questions.
- Skim first for the main idea. The first and last sentences of the passage often tell you the topic and the conclusion.
- For detail questions, find the key words in the question, locate them in the passage, and read the sentence before and after.
- For vocabulary questions, replace the word with each option and check which keeps the meaning of the sentence.
- For inference questions, choose the option that must be true based on the text, not one that might be true.
- For purpose questions ("Why does the author mention..."), ask what job the detail does: an example, a contrast, evidence for a claim.
## How wrong options are built
Understanding how test writers create wrong options is one of the best tricks you can learn.
- Copied words: the option repeats words from the passage but says something different. Correct options usually paraphrase.
- Reversed: the option says the opposite, or switches cause and effect.
- Too extreme: "always", "never", "all", "completely" when the passage says "often" or "some".
- Not mentioned: sounds reasonable but the passage does not say it.
- True but does not answer the question: correct according to the passage, but about a different point.
- Mixes two details: combines information from two parts of the passage in a way the text does not support.

> Passage: "Some early farmers kept cattle mainly for milk rather than meat." Wrong option: "Early farmers kept cattle mainly for meat." (reversed). Wrong option: "All early farmers kept cattle." (too extreme). Correct option: "For some early farmers, milk was the main reason to raise cattle." (paraphrase).
! If an option copies a long phrase from the passage word for word, be suspicious. Check it carefully before you choose it.
## Timing
- Keep moving. If an item takes much longer than the others, choose your best answer and go on.
- Check the timer at about the halfway point of each module.
- Answer every item, even if you have to guess at the end.
## Building reading skill between mocks
- Read one short academic article a day (science news, history, psychology) and write a one-sentence summary.
- Practice word families for Complete the Words.
- When you review a practice set, write down why each wrong option is wrong. This trains you to see the traps quickly.

articles.title: Listening tips and tricks
lines: The Listening section has 47 items in about 29 minutes, in a router module and then a lower or upper module. Every recording is played once, and the questions come after it. It includes four types of task: Listen and Choose a Response, conversations, announcements and academic talks.
## Listen and Choose a Response
You hear a single line, such as a question, an offer, a complaint or a piece of news, and choose the best reply from four written options.
- First decide what kind of line it is. A question? A request? An invitation? Bad news?

- The correct reply often answers indirectly. "Are you coming to the review session?" "I've got a shift at the café until six." The speaker does not say yes or no, but the meaning is clear: probably not.
- Watch for traps: a reply with a word that sounds like a word in the line, a reply in the wrong tense or person, a reply to a different question, or a reply that is socially odd.
> Line: "Could you send me the notes from today's lecture?"
> Good reply: "Sure, I'll email them to you tonight."
> Trap: "The lecture was about climate." (answers a different question)
> Trap: "Yes, I sent them yesterday." (wrong time: the lecture was today)
! Read all four options before choosing. Two may seem possible, and only one fits the tone and the time of the line.
## Conversations
Conversations are between two people on campus or in daily life: a student and an advisor, two classmates, a customer and an employee.
- Listen for the problem or reason at the start. Gist questions ask why the person is talking to the other.
- Notice the options discussed and the final decision. The first suggestion is not always the one chosen.
- Listen for feelings and attitude: tone of voice, words like "unfortunately", "honestly", "I'm a bit worried".
- "What will the woman probably do next?" is usually answered near the end.
## Announcements
An announcement gives information to a group: a schedule change, a new rule, an event.
- Note what is happening, when, and what listeners need to do.
- Expect one key instruction, often after words like "please make sure", "remember to", "you'll need to".
- Notice any changes or exceptions: "instead of", "this week only", "except for".
## Academic talks
Short lecture-style talks on university subjects such as biology, geology, art history or economics.
- The topic usually comes in the first few sentences. Write it down.
- Listen for the structure: a definition, then examples; a problem, then explanations; a comparison of two ideas.
- At least one question usually asks about the main idea or why the speaker mentions an example. When you hear an example, ask yourself what point it supports.
- Expect paraphrase. The correct option will rarely use the exact words of the speaker.

> Speaker: "Take the Arctic fox. In winter its coat is white, and by summer it turns brown." Question: Why does the speaker mention the Arctic fox? Correct option: to give an example of an animal whose color changes with the seasons. Trap: to explain why foxes live in cold regions.
## Understanding natural speech
Recordings sound like real speech: contractions, linking, hesitation and changes of mind.
- Learn common reductions: gonna (going to), wanna (want to), gotta (got to), kinda (kind of), lemme (let me).
- Notice linking: "turn it off" sounds like "tur-ni-toff".
- Pay attention to stress. The word a speaker stresses is usually important.
- Listen for self-corrections: "The meeting is on Tuesday, oh wait, no, it's Wednesday." The second fact is the right one.
! When a speaker says "actually", "but" or "to be honest", the important information usually follows.
## During the test
- Use the few seconds before each recording to look at any context on screen.
- Take short notes (see "Note-taking for Listening").
- Answer quickly after the recording. Your memory is freshest right away.
- If you missed the answer, eliminate what you know is wrong, guess and move on. The next recording needs all your attention.
## Building listening skill between mocks
- Listen to English for 20-30 minutes a day: university lecture videos, science podcasts, interviews.
- Mix accents. The TOEFL uses speakers from different English-speaking regions.
- Practice "shadowing": play a short clip and repeat it at the same time as the speaker. It improves both listening and Listen and Repeat in Speaking.
- After practice sets, replay the parts you missed (in this app, review the script) and find the exact sentence that gave the answer.

articles.title: Writing tips: Build a Sentence, email and discussion templates
lines: The Writing section has 12 items in 23 minutes: ten Build a Sentence items, one Write an Email task and one Write for an Academic Discussion task. Each needs a different skill, so practice them separately and then together under time.
## Build a Sentence
You see a short exchange and a reply made of word chunks in the wrong order. You put the chunks in order to make one correct, natural sentence. Some items include an extra chunk that does not belong.
- Read the first line of the exchange. The reply must answer it.
- Find the subject and main verb first, then build around them.

- Check question order: in a direct question the auxiliary comes before the subject ("Did you finish..."); in an indirect question the subject comes before the verb ("Do you know where the office is?").
- Place adverbs of frequency before the main verb and after "be": "She usually arrives early", "He is always on time".
- Look for fixed patterns: "not only ... but also", "so ... that", "the reason why", relative clauses with who, which and that.
- If there is an extra chunk, it is often a duplicate preposition, a wrong auxiliary (does instead of did) or a wrong word form.
> Exchange: "Where should I submit the form?" Chunks: [the office] [you can] [it at] [leave] [on the second floor]
> Answer: You can leave it at the office on the second floor.
! Read your finished sentence silently from start to end. If it sounds wrong in your head, it probably is.
## Write an Email (7 minutes)

You read a situation and three points you must cover. The reader might be a professor, a manager, a landlord or a customer service team. You are scored on how clearly and politely you complete the task and on your language.
- Cover all three points. Missing one is the most expensive mistake.
- Match the tone to the reader: polite and formal for a professor, friendly but clear for a classmate.
- Give specific details. "The heater in my room has not worked since Monday" is better than "There is a problem".
- In our experience, a good email in 7 minutes is usually about 120 to 180 words. Quality and completeness matter more than length.
Template (adapt it, do not copy it word for word in every email):
> Dear Professor Chen,
> I am writing about [reason]. [One or two sentences of context.]
> [Point 1: explain the problem or situation with a detail.]
> [Point 2: make your request politely. "Would it be possible to...?" "I would be grateful if you could..."]
> [Point 3: suggest a solution or give extra details. "If that is not possible, I could..."]
> Thank you for your time and help. I look forward to hearing from you.
> Best regards,
> Priya
Useful phrases:
- Explaining: "Unfortunately, ...", "The reason I am writing is that...", "I have noticed that..."
- Requesting: "Would it be possible to...?", "Could you let me know whether...?", "I would appreciate it if..."
- Suggesting: "One option might be to...", "Perhaps we could...", "I would be happy to..."
- Closing: "Thank you in advance.", "Please let me know if you need any further information."
! Do not start every sentence with "I". Vary your openings: "Unfortunately", "Because of this", "If possible", "In addition".
## Write for an Academic Discussion (10 minutes)
A professor posts a question to an online class. Two students reply with different views. You write your own contribution.
- Read the professor's question carefully. What exactly is being asked?
- Choose a position quickly. Pick the side you can support best, not the side you think is "correct".
- Add something new. Do not just repeat what the students said. Give a new reason or a new example.
- Refer to at least one student by name to show you are taking part in the discussion.
- An effective response is usually at least 100 words. Aim for about 120 to 150 well-organized words.
Template:
> [Position] In my view, ... / I believe ... because ...
> [Link to a student] Mateo makes a good point about ..., but I think he overlooks ... / I agree with Aisha that ..., and I would add that ...
> [New reason] The main reason is that ...
> [Example] For example, in my own city / at my school / in a study I read about, ...
> [Closing] For these reasons, I think ...
> Example contribution (topic: should universities require first-year students to live on campus?):

> I believe first-year students should be encouraged, but not required, to live on campus. Sofia argues that dormitory life helps new students make friends, and that is true for many people. However, I think she overlooks the cost. For some families, a dormitory is much more expensive than living at home, and a rule like this could stop talented students from enrolling. A better approach would be to offer social events and study groups for students who commute, so they can build friendships too. For example, my cousin's college runs evening clubs for commuters, and they are always full. For these reasons, a flexible policy seems fairer.
## Checking your writing in the last minute
- Did you answer every part of the task?
- Verb tenses and subject-verb agreement (he has, they have).
- Articles (a, an, the) and plurals.
- Spelling of key words from the prompt. Copy them correctly.
- One idea per sentence. Split very long sentences.
## Practice routine
- Build a Sentence: one set of 10 a day for a week, timed. Note the grammar point of each mistake.
- Email: three emails a week, then compare with the model and the checklist.
- Discussion: three posts a week. Before writing, list two possible new reasons in 30 seconds. This trains fast planning.

articles.title: Speaking tips: Listen and Repeat and the Interview
lines: The Speaking section has 11 items in only 8 minutes: seven Listen and Repeat sentences and four Take an Interview questions, with 45 seconds for each interview answer. It is short, so every second counts.
## Listen and Repeat

You hear a sentence and repeat it as accurately as you can. The sentences usually relate to one situation, such as a guide or a manager giving instructions, and they get longer, from a few words to long sentences with clauses.
- Listen to the meaning, not just the sounds. It is much easier to remember "Please leave your bags in the lockers near the entrance" as an idea than as a string of words.
- Notice the structure: an instruction, a time clause ("before you leave"), a relative clause ("the room that is on your left"), numbers and place names.
- Repeat at a natural speed with natural stress. Do not speak word by word.
- Keep small grammar words: the, a, to, of, -s, -ed. They are often what separates a good repeat from a weak one.
- If you forget a word, do not stop. Say the sentence as completely as you can, with a natural word in the gap.
> Original: "If the printer runs out of paper, you'll find more in the cabinet next to the window."
> Weak repeat: "If printer out of paper, find more in cabinet window."
> Strong repeat: "If the printer runs out of paper, you'll find more in the cabinet next to the window."
! Chunk long sentences into two or three meaning groups as you listen: "If the printer runs out of paper / you'll find more / in the cabinet next to the window." Repeat them group by group.
## Take an Interview
An interviewer asks four questions on one topic. The questions usually move from your own experience to opinions, comparisons and predictions. You have 45 seconds for each answer.
A simple answer pattern:
- Answer directly in the first sentence.
- Give one reason.
- Give one specific example from your life or something you know.
- If time remains, add a comparison or a short conclusion.
> Question: How do you usually prepare for an important exam?

> Answer: I usually start about two weeks before the exam by making a simple schedule. The main reason is that I get nervous if I leave everything to the last minute. For example, before my chemistry exam last year, I studied one chapter each evening and used the weekend for practice questions. It worked really well, and I felt calm on the day. I'd say planning ahead is the most important thing for me.
Useful spoken phrases:
- Opinion: "I'd say...", "Personally, I think...", "In my experience..."
- Reason: "The main reason is that...", "That's because..."
- Example: "For example...", "Take my brother, for instance..."
- Comparison: "Compared with ten years ago...", "Unlike in big cities..."
- Prediction: "I expect that...", "In the future, I think we'll probably..."
- Buying time naturally: "That's an interesting question.", "Let me think... I'd say..."
! Do not memorize full answers. Interviewers ask specific questions, and a memorized speech that does not fit sounds unnatural. Memorize the pattern and the phrases instead.
## Fluency and pronunciation
- Speak at a steady, comfortable pace. Fast speech with many errors is harder to understand than calm, clear speech.
- Use contractions: I'm, it's, I'd, don't. They sound natural.
- Pause at the end of ideas, not in the middle of phrases.
- Stress key words: "I REALLY think the LIBRARY should stay open LATER."
- Clear pronunciation matters more than accent. You do not need to sound American.
## Using the 45 seconds well
- Do not stop at 20 seconds. A full answer shows more of your English.
- Do not try to say everything. One clear reason and one good example are better than four vague points.
- If you finish your example and there is time left, add a comparison or explain what you learned.
## Practice routine
- Shadowing: 5-10 minutes a day. Play a short English clip and speak along with it. This builds memory and rhythm for Listen and Repeat.
- Record yourself. Listen back and check grammar words, endings and clarity.
- Interview practice: pick a topic (food, travel, technology, study habits) and answer four questions in the same order: experience, opinion, comparison, prediction. Time every answer at 45 seconds.
- Keep a list of mistakes you make often (see "Common mistakes South Asian test takers make") and listen for them in your recordings.

articles.title: Using your mock results
lines: A mock test is only useful if you learn from it. Taking mock after mock without reviewing them is like weighing yourself every day without changing your diet. This article gives you a review method that turns each mock into a clear plan for the next week.
## Right after the mock
- Write down the bands for each section and the overall band.
- Write down which module you reached in Reading and in Listening (lower or upper).
- Write one sentence about how it felt: where you ran short of time, where you lost focus, which tasks felt hard.
Do this immediately, while you remember. The feelings are useful data.
Then do the full review, which takes 60-90 minutes, on the same day or the next.
## Step 1: Sort your mistakes in Reading and Listening
For each wrong answer, decide which kind of mistake it was:
- Vocabulary: I did not know a key word.
- Understanding: I misunderstood the sentence or the speaker.
- Trap: I chose an option that copied words, reversed the idea or was too extreme.
- Careless: I knew the answer but clicked or typed the wrong thing.
- Time: I guessed because I was running out of time.
- Missed it: in Listening, I did not hear or did not note the key point.

> Example tally for Listening: Vocabulary 2, Understanding 3, Trap 4, Careless 1, Time 0, Missed it 5. The biggest groups are Missed it and Trap. Next week: note-taking practice with signal words, and reviewing wrong options in every practice set.
## Step 2: Look at task types

Go through your answers by task type (Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life, academic passages, and so on) and find the one or two task types with the lowest accuracy. Those are your targets. For example, if Complete the Words is much lower than the academic passages, your spelling and word forms need work.
## Step 3: Review Writing
- Compare your email and discussion post with the model answers.
- Check: did you cover every point? Did you add a new idea in the discussion? Did you mention a student by name?
- Count your three most frequent grammar mistakes and add them to your personal mistakes list.
- For Build a Sentence, write down the grammar point behind each wrong item.
## Step 4: Review Speaking
- Listen to your recordings if the app saved them.
- For Listen and Repeat, compare word by word: which words did you drop? Usually it is small words and endings.
- For the Interview, check: did you answer in the first sentence? Did you give a reason and an example? Did you use most of the 45 seconds?
## Step 5: Make the plan
Choose no more than three goals for the next week. Make each one specific and measurable.
> Weak goal: "Improve listening."
> Strong goal: "Practice 2 academic talks a day with notes of 15 words or fewer; review every missed main idea question."
> Strong goal: "20 minutes of word families every day for Complete the Words."
> Strong goal: "Write 3 discussion posts with a timer, each with a new reason and a student's name."
## Reading the trend
- One mock is one data point. Scores go up and down by half a band for many reasons: the topics, your sleep, your mood.
- Look at the trend over three or more mocks. A steady rise of half a band over a month is real progress.
- If a section has stayed flat for three mocks, change the method for that section, not just the amount of practice.
- If you reach the upper module more often, that is a sign of progress even if the band has not moved yet.
## When to book or keep your test date
- If your last two or three mocks are at or above your target band, you are probably ready.
- If you are within half a band, a few weeks of focused work on your weakest section often closes the gap.
- If you are more than a band below target, consider moving the date and following the 8-week plan.
! Mock scores in any practice app are estimates, not official ETS scores. Use them to guide your study, and keep a small safety margin above your target.
## Keep a simple log

A single page or note with columns for date, Reading, Listening, Writing, Speaking, overall, module reached and your three goals is enough. Reading it before each mock shows you what to focus on and reminds you how far you have come.

articles.title: 4-week and 8-week study plans
lines: These two plans assume you can study about 1 to 2 hours a day, six days a week, with one day off. Choose the 4-week plan if your first mock is within about half a band of your target, and the 8-week plan if the gap is larger or you are new to the TOEFL. Adjust the plan with the results of each mock (see "Using your mock results").
## Every day, in both plans
- Vocabulary: 15 minutes with the flashcards (10 new words plus review).
- Listening: 10-20 minutes of English audio (lectures, podcasts, interviews), with 5 minutes of shadowing.
- One section practice set from the app, timed.
## The 4-week plan
## Week 1: Diagnose and learn the tasks
- Day 1: full mock. Review it with the 5-step method.
- Days 2-3: read the lessons for every Reading and Listening task type and do one practice set of each.
- Days 4-5: read the Writing and Speaking lessons. Write one email and one discussion post. Record four interview answers.
- Day 6: redo the task types you scored lowest on. Write your personal mistakes list.
## Week 2: Work on your weakest section
- Spend about half of your study time on your weakest section and the rest on the others.
- Reading weak: two Complete the Words sets and two academic passage sets a day, with wrong-option review.
- Listening weak: two academic talks and one conversation a day, with notes of 15 words or fewer.
- Writing weak: one email or discussion post a day, plus one Build a Sentence set.
- Speaking weak: Listen and Repeat practice daily, plus four interview answers on a new topic.
- Day 6: full mock and review.
## Week 3: Speed and the second weakest section
- Do all practice sets with a timer. Aim to finish with a little time left.
- Move half of your focus to your second weakest section.
- Practice the email and discussion templates until you can plan each one in a minute.
- Day 6: full mock in one sitting at the time of day of your real test.
## Week 4: Polish and rest
- Days 1-3: mixed practice sets from every section; review your mistakes list daily.
- Day 4: final full mock, at least two days before the test.
- Day 5: light review of templates, phrases and mistakes. No new material.
- Day 6: rest, prepare ID and route or Home Edition setup, sleep early.
## The 8-week plan
## Weeks 1-2: Foundations
- Day 1: full mock and review.
- Learn every task type with the lessons and one practice set each.
- Grammar focus: articles, verb tenses, question word order and prepositions (see "Common mistakes South Asian test takers make"). 20 minutes a day.
- Build the reading habit: one short academic article a day with a one-sentence summary.
- End of week 2: section practice under time for Reading and Listening.
## Weeks 3-4: Reading and Listening skills
- Daily Reading: one Complete the Words set and one academic passage set; learn the wrong-option types.
- Daily Listening: two recordings with notes; practice signal words.
- Writing and Speaking: two emails, two discussion posts and two interview sessions per week.
- End of week 4: full mock and review. Set three new goals.
## Weeks 5-6: Writing and Speaking skills, plus speed
- Writing: one email or discussion post a day, checked against the model and your mistakes list.
- Build a Sentence: one set a day until you can finish quickly with few mistakes.
- Speaking: daily Listen and Repeat and shadowing; four interview answers on a new topic every other day.
- Reading and Listening: keep up with one timed set of each a day.
- End of week 6: full mock and review.
## Week 7: Full-test practice
- Two full mocks this week, in one sitting each, at the time of your real test.
- Between mocks, work only on what the mocks show is weak.
## Week 8: Polish and rest
- Same as week 4 of the 4-week plan: mixed practice, a final mock at least two days before the test, then light review and rest.
## Adapting the plans
- If you can study only 30-45 minutes a day, stretch each plan to about double the length.
- If one section is already at your target, keep it fresh with two practice sets a week and spend the rest on the others.
- If you reach your target in two mocks in a row before the plan ends, you can book or keep an earlier test date.
! Consistency beats intensity. One focused hour every day for four weeks does more than two long weekends of cramming.
